contact-lens-hygiene-break.text: Users pause lens wear and clean lenses carefully to get clearer, whiter-looking eyes. It appears in looksmaxxing lists under eye whites. Lens-related redness is a recognised clinical topic, but no study tests this routine for appearance.

chest-resonance-training.text: Users practise speaking from the chest to sound deeper and fuller, borrowing the chest voice idea from singing instruction. Acoustics sources describe the chest as adding little resonance, and the appearance use itself has not been trialled.

lowering-pitch-exercises.text: Users train a lower speaking pitch to sound deeper or more masculine without surgery or drugs. Pitch is measurable and voice training is studied in clinical settings, but trials for this appearance goal are absent.

vocal-fry-and-glottal-control.text: Some users control vocal fry to make their voice sound lower. Perception studies of creaky voice exist, but none test it as a way to improve vocal attractiveness.

diaphragmatic-breathing.text: Users practise belly breathing to support the voice and speak with more depth and presence. It is studied for stress and respiratory care, while its effect on how a voice sounds in appearance terms is untested.

voice-coach-speech-therapy.text: People hire voice coaches or speech-language pathologists to change pitch, quality and delivery, a route also used in transgender voice therapy. The clinical field is real and established; trials specific to looksmaxxing goals are absent.

singing-lessons.text: Users take singing lessons to gain voice control, range and a deeper or more resonant speaking voice. Singing instruction is studied for wellbeing and lung function, not for changing how a speaking voice comes across.

humming-exercises.text: Users hum as a vocal warm-up before speaking or singing to get a smoother, more resonant sound. It is popular in voice-training circles, with little research on appearance-related outcomes.

straw-phonation.text: Users voice through a narrow straw as a warm-up and training drill for a clearer, more controlled voice. It belongs to SOVT exercises with real clinical research; vocal attractiveness has not been tested.

resonance-tuning-formant.text: Voice-improvement communities adjust vocal tract shape to move formants and change timbre, aiming for a deeper or more masculine sound. Formant acoustics is well established; the practice as a looksmaxxing method is untested.

pitch-tracking-apps.text: Users run pitch tracking apps to see their speaking pitch in Hz while practising a deeper or more resonant voice. They work as a measuring tool; no studies link their use to appearance outcomes.

testosterone-replacement-therapy.text: Medical testosterone is used to restore normal levels in hypogonadism, and users in appearance circles note its virilizing effects including a deeper voice and added muscle. It is studied for muscle and metabolic outcomes in hypogonadal men, not as a voice treatment.

testosterone-cypionate.text: Testosterone cypionate is a long-acting injectable labelled for hypogonadism, with voice deepening listed among its virilizing effects. Voice change is a side effect of androgen action rather than a studied purpose.

anavar-oxandrolone-voice-risk.text: Oxandrolone (Anavar) is an oral anabolic steroid used for muscle and physique; its documented virilizing effects in women include voice deepening, which can be irreversible. Voice change here is an off-target effect, not a studied goal.

anabolic-steroids-for-voice.text: Androgens including anabolic steroids can lower the voice by acting on the larynx, and some users seek this effect. It is a documented side effect of virilization rather than a studied use, and some changes may be permanent.

hcg-and-clomiphene-for-voice.text: Forum users mention hCG and clomiphene as ways to raise natural testosterone in the hope of a deeper voice. Both are used medically for fertility and off-label for male hypogonadism; no studies address voice.

tongue-posture-for-voice.text: Looksmaxxing communities extend mewing to the voice, proposing that tongue posture changes resonance. The base mewing claim concerns jaw structure and is unproven, and no voice study exists.

throat-singing-practice.text: Users borrow Tuvan kargyraa and similar overtone singing to train a lower, more resonant voice. The techniques are well documented traditions, but their effect on ordinary speech has not been tested.

vocal-cord-filler-injection.text: Injection laryngoplasty adds bulk to a vocal fold so the folds meet better, and appearance-focused communities discuss it for a fuller voice. Evidence comes from medical use in vocal fold paralysis and weakness, not cosmetic voice change.

laryngoplasty-adam-s-apple-surgery.text: Chondrolaryngoplasty (tracheal shave) shaves the thyroid cartilage so the Adam's apple is visibly flatter, and is sought for a more feminine neck contour. The result is directly visible, and published series report mostly satisfied patients.

voice-surgery-cricothyroid-approximation.text: Cricothyroid approximation raises pitch by tensioning the vocal folds and has mainly been used for voice feminisation. The pitch change is measurable after surgery; newer techniques have largely replaced it.

adam-s-apple-enhancement.text: Surgical enlargement of the Adam's apple adds a visible neck prominence, described mainly as part of facial masculinization for transmasculine patients. The change is directly visible; evidence is a handful of small case series.

neck-training-for-voice.text: Looksmaxxing communities propose that strengthening and thickening the neck deepens the voice, alongside a thicker-looking neck. No published studies test the voice claim.

hydration-and-humidifier-for-voice.text: Users drink water and humidify rooms to keep vocal folds moist for a clearer, smoother voice. Hydration has been examined with vocal rest in relation to vocal fatigue in karaoke singers; appearance outcomes are untested.

throat-coat-tea.text: Singers and voice-conscious users drink slippery-elm herbal teas such as Throat Coat for throat comfort and a smoother voice. Use is traditional; no clinical studies of these teas were found.

honey-and-ginger-throat-soothing.text: Users take honey and ginger in warm drinks to soothe the throat and keep the voice comfortable. Honey has some cough data and WHO guidance for sore throats, while ginger rests on traditional use; voice appearance is untested.

vocal-rest.text: Users rest the voice after strain to recover a clear, steady sound. Vocal rest appears in vocal hygiene guidance for voice professionals and sits within research on vocal fatigue; its effect on voice appearance is untested.

avoiding-whispering.text: Users speak softly instead of whispering to reduce strain and protect voice quality. The advice appears in voice-care discussion and rests on limited, indirect evidence.

treating-acid-reflux-for-voice.text: Users manage laryngopharyngeal reflux to relieve hoarseness and improve voice quality. Treatment studies for LPR are mixed and the diagnosis is debated; effects on voice appearance specifically are untested.

quit-smoking-for-voice.text: Users quit smoking to avoid or reverse hoarseness and the lowered, rougher pitch linked to smoking. Smoking is a documented cause of vocal fold swelling, though studies focus on health rather than voice attractiveness.
